title: Sorted input makes a chain
summary: The same five values, inserted in two orders, give two very different trees.

checkpoints.text: The values arrive sorted. Each new one is larger than everything already in the tree, so it always goes right.
The "tree" is a straight line: every node has only a right child. It is still a valid binary search tree, but it behaves like a linked list.
The same values in a different order. 30 arrives first and splits the rest into a left and a right side.
Searching the chain for 50 has to pass every node, one by one.

checkpoints.at: cout << "Bushy: height " << height(bushy) << ", finding 50 takes " << comparisons(bushy, 50) << " comparisons" << endl;
checkpoints.text: Chain: height 5 and 5 comparisons. Bushy: height 3 and 3 comparisons. A search costs as much as the tree is tall, so a chain makes it O(n) instead of O(log n). AVL trees exist to stop this from happening.
